package.title: Slowing AI Could Speed Up the Economy
package.promised: A case that slowing down AI adoption or requiring human checks can make the economy more productive rather than less. I expect to learn why AI still needs people in the workflow and what economic benefit comes from that restraint.

new_things: AI can create a second job of supervising it.
Less supervision lets existing AI models finish more work.
The speaker sees an economic opportunity in slowing the AI frontier.
Dario Amodei is associated with Anthropic.
reports.held_question: Why would slowing the AI frontier create that economic opportunity?

new_things: Anthropic's Dario Amodei has argued for slowing or pacing frontier AI development.
The suggested priority is improving systems that actually finish work rather than pushing the frontier.
A useful handoff should complete work instead of leaving the user with a checklist.
reports.held_question: Will the handoff actually finish the work, or just leave me with a checklist?
could_not_follow: The final sentence cut off after 'One missed handoff makes a...'

new_things: A missed handoff makes someone inspect the output, repair it, and run the chain again.
The example job has twenty required steps.
Each step is assumed to succeed independently 95 percent of the time.
The example allows no retries or recovery.
reports.held_question: How likely is the whole twenty-step job to finish successfully under those assumptions?

new_things: With twenty independent steps that each succeed 95 percent of the time and no recovery, the clean completion rate is 36 percent.
Those figures are an illustration, not a measurement of a real product.
If each of the same twenty steps succeeds 99 percent of the time, clean completion rises to 82 percent.
A small improvement at each step can let many more jobs finish cleanly.
Fewer failures may mean fewer human rescues.
The saved human time could go toward work that ships and serving customers, allowing the team to produce more.
reports.held_question: How do memory and tools fit into improving this process?

new_things: Memory, tools, and error checks count as development work.
A stronger frontier model might reduce the need for human supervision and should be tested the same way.
If reliability matters most, a slower frontier model could still make the overall process faster.
reports.held_question: Can a stronger frontier model save the same human hours by reducing supervision?

new_things: The economy could speed up even if the frontier model itself is slower.
Demo cleverness is not the measure to use.
The human follow-up job ends when the AI completes the original job.
reports.held_question: How should AI be judged if not by how clever its demos look?
